Means of Sanctification
MEENZ uv SANK-tih-fih-KAY-shun
noun phrase
From Middle English mene (method, instrument, from Old French moyen and Latin medianus, middle, intermediary) + Latin sanctificatio (a setting apart, making holy, from sanctus holy + facere to make). The phrase names the specific instruments or channels through which the Holy Spirit progressively works holiness in the regenerate believer—a subdivision of the broader category of the means of grace.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The means of sanctification are the appointed instruments through which the Holy Spirit progressively works the holiness of God into the regenerate soul. Unlike the means of grace in their widest sense (which include the instruments of conversion), the means of sanctification address the ongoing work of mortification and vivification in the believer after regeneration. Scripture identifies the Word of God as the primary instrument: Christ prays, “Sanctify them in the truth. Your word is truth” (John 17:17), and Paul teaches that the washing of water “with the word” is the instrument by which Christ sanctifies His church (Eph. 5:26). The indwelling Spirit applies this Word, convicting of remaining sin (Rom. 8:13), producing the fruit of the Spirit (Gal. 5:22–23), and conforming the believer to the image of Christ (Rom. 8:29). Prayer sustains and directs the sanctifying work (Phil. 4:6–7). The Lord’s Supper, rightly received, nourishes sanctifying grace by proclaiming the Lord’s death and drawing the believer into communion with the crucified and risen Christ (1 Cor. 11:26; 10:16). Corporate worship, preaching, Christian fellowship, and the exercise of discipline all function as means through which God pursues the holiness He requires. The apostle grounds the believer’s cooperation in divine enabling: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who is at work in you” (Phil. 2:12–13). Sanctification is thus synergistic in form but monergistic in source: the believer strives, but the Spirit empowers every genuine striving. The 1689 Confession (13.1–3) and Westminster Confession (13.1–3) both affirm that sanctification is real, progressive, and accomplished through the same Word and Spirit that accomplished regeneration.

Webster 1828 Definition

Means of sanctification: the appointed instruments — chiefly the Word, prayer, the ordinances, and Christian fellowship — through which the Holy Spirit progressively works holiness into the soul of the regenerate believer.

expand to see more

MEANS, noun. plural. (Theology) The instruments or channels appointed by God for conveying grace; the ordinary means of grace include the Word of God preached and read, prayer, baptism, and the Lord’s Supper; the means of sanctification are those among them most directly concerned with the progressive holiness of the regenerate.

SANCTIFICATION, noun. (Theology) The work of God’s free grace whereby we are renewed in the whole man after the image of God, and are enabled more and more to die unto sin and live unto righteousness (1689 Confession 13.1).

2. Distinguished from justification: sanctification is not the ground of acceptance before God (that is justification by imputed righteousness alone) but the necessary fruit of genuine justification—faith without works is dead (James 2:17), and progressive holiness without which no man shall see the Lord (Heb. 12:14).

3. The believer’s cooperation: Phil. 2:12–13 holds human striving and divine enabling in their proper order—work out, because God works in; the striver does not earn the grace but receives it through the means God has appointed.

Key Scripture

John 17:17 — "Sanctify them in the truth. Your word is truth."

Philippians 2:12 — "Therefore, my beloved, just as you have always obeyed — not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence — work out your salvation with fear and trembling."

Philippians 2:13 — "For it is God who is at work in you — both to will and to work for His good pleasure."

1 Thessalonians 4:3 — "For this is the will of God: your sanctification — that you abstain from sexual immorality;"

Modern Corruption

Both antinomianism (rejecting the law’s sanctifying role) and moralism (seeking holiness through will-power without the Spirit) corrupt the biblical means of sanctification by severing the instrument from the divine Agent who alone makes it effective.

expand to see more

Antinomianism in its various forms (historical, Keswick quietist, and modern “let go and let God” passive spirituality) refuses the believer’s active cooperation in sanctification by treating striving as a threat to grace. But the apostolic command is unambiguous: “work out your salvation with fear and trembling” (Phil. 2:12). The promise of divine enabling (Phil. 2:13) does not eliminate the command but grounds it. Where antinomianism says “simply trust and the Spirit does the rest,” Scripture says “be killing sin or it will be killing you” (John Owen). Passivity before remaining sin is not faith but negligence; the means of sanctification are means precisely because God intends the believer to use them diligently.

The opposite corruption is moralism: the attempt to achieve holiness through disciplined willpower, religious habit, or behavioral modification without the Spirit’s transforming work. Modern therapeutic self-improvement programs—including many marketed as “biblical”—reduce sanctification to behavior change, skill acquisition, or identity reconstruction, bypassing the Spirit’s conviction, the Word’s searching power, and the cross’s mortifying grace. The result is external conformity without inward transformation—the Pharisee’s religion, which Jesus diagnosed as whitewashed tombs full of dead men’s bones (Matt. 23:27). True sanctification requires both the means (Word, prayer, ordinances, fellowship) and the Agent (the Holy Spirit), neither of which may be bypassed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin medianus (intermediary) and sanctificatio (making holy) name the ordained instruments that the Holy Spirit uses as channels of progressive holiness—not automatic mechanisms but Spirit-empowered means requiring the believer’s diligent use.

expand to see more

Greek hagiasmos — sanctification, holiness; from hagios (holy, set apart); the NT noun for the progressive work of consecration that follows regeneration and culminates in glorification

Latin instrumentum — tool, instrument; the means of sanctification are not self-operating mechanisms but Spirit-wielded instruments—the Spirit uses the Word as a surgeon uses a scalpel, with precision and purpose

Hebrew qadash — to consecrate, set apart, make holy; the OT root of sanctification—Israel’s holiness was mediated through the law (Lev. 19:2; “be holy, for I am holy”) just as the church’s holiness is mediated through the Word

Greek renō / Latin renovatio — renewal, renovation; the Reformed description of sanctification as the progressive renewal of the whole man (1689 Conf. 13.1)—not mere behavior modification but renovation of mind, will, and affections

Greek teleioō — to complete, perfect, bring to the goal; Hebrews uses this word for Christ as the “author and finisher of faith” (Heb. 12:2)—sanctification’s telos is conformity to Christ, which the Spirit pursues through the appointed means

Usage

"The Puritans’ rich literature on mortification (John Owen, Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers; Richard Sibbes, The Bruised Reed) is essentially a theology of the means of sanctification: how the Word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, and Christian fellowship operate as the Spirit’s instruments for killing indwelling sin."

"Corporate worship functions as a means of sanctification through the combined operation of preaching (the Word applied), singing (the Word embodied in praise), prayer (the Word addressed back to God), and the Supper (the Word enacted in sacramental form)—each reinforcing the others."

"The believer who neglects the appointed means of sanctification—forsaking the assembly (Heb. 10:25), prayerlessness, inattentiveness to the Word—does not remain spiritually static; remaining sin advances where grace is not actively cultivated through the Spirit’s instruments."
